Theme

Body, health & movement

fever noun

also temperature, have a temperature, run a fever, hot forehead, do you have a fever?, high fever, run a high fever, the fever goes down, constant fever, slight fever

classical

Traupman 64
M-O s.v. fever
Traupman 55: frōns et genae sunt calidae
Traupman 56: febrem magnam habēre, to run a high fever
Traupman 314

1febris: e left unmarked (Lewis & Short fē^bris, marking the e as common, “the ē predominating in poets”). The poets’ long scansion may only reflect the heavy syllable before -br-, and de Vaan (s.v. febris) does not discuss the quantity.

febris1, febris f.

noun, third declension · Declension on Wiktionary

Accusative febrim or febrem.

Other words

  • febrīcula, febrīculae f. — a slight temperature

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 12.1.2, of his little daughter Attica: dē Atticae febrīculā … valdē doluī; Traupman 314 · Declension on Wiktionary

    Long ī (L&S).

  • febrīcitāre — run a fever

    also used · classical · Traupman 64; Cels., post-Augustan; Traupman 314

    Long ī (L&S).

  • conquiēscō, conquiēscere, conquiēvī — go down, subside (of a fever)

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Cels. 2.8: febris (Lewis & Short); Traupman 322 · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    Celsus’ word for a fever or an inflammation that subsides: febris conquiēscit, the fever goes down.

Examples

  • febrim habēre

    have a feverCic. Fam. 7.26.1

  • in febrim incidere

    get a feverCic. Fam. 14.8.1

  • Frōns calida est.

    Your forehead is hot.composed

  • Febrim habēs; hodiē domī manēbimus.

    You’ve got a temperature; we’ll stay home today.composed

  • continua febris

    a constant feverTraupman 314

  • magna (ārdēns) febris

    a high feverTraupman 314

See also ill, shiver, forehead.
